previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old male with a history of psoriatic arthritis, chronic steroid use, and adrenal insufficiency was admitted for severe fluid retention and weight gain, primarily in the abdomen, causing shortness of breath. He was found to have acute kidney injury likely due to a recent steroid taper and aggressive diuresis in the outpatient cardiology clinic. After stabilization of kidney function, he was treated with a furosemide drip and boluses, resulting in 28 liters of fluid output over nine days, but only a 6 kg weight loss, a discrepancy that remains unexplained. Hypokalemia was managed with supplementation and deemed diuretic-induced. Diuretics were discontinued at discharge due to the inconsistent response. The patient was discharged home with an increased dexamethasone dose, off all diuretics and potassium supplements, and with close follow-up to reassess fluid management.
problems: Acute kidney failure with lesion of tubular necrosis
Adrenal cortical steroids causing adverse effects in therapeutic use
Diabetes mellitus without mention of complication, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled
Unspecified hereditary and idiopathic peripheral neuropathy

# HYPOKALEMIA: Pt has h/o recurrent episodes of hypokalemia. At 
times, this has been hypothesized to be due to diarrhea or use 
of diuretics. Pt had been off diuretics for past week since 
discharge to the hospital. He has been followed by endocrine 
(last seen in clinic on day PTA), who have felt to this point 
that hypokalemia is due to diuretics. Per endocrine consult this 
hospitalization, it may be that his hypokalemia is caused by the 
persistence of diuretics in his system, and will take a bit 
longer for them all to be excreted. However, also per 
endocrinology cannot completely rule out primary 
hyperaldosteronism. Nephrology consult suggested DDx of primary 
hyperaldosteronism vs. Gitelman's syndrome vs. surreptitious 
diuretic use. Gitelman's syndrome possible because pt had 
grandmother with chronic hypokalemia requiring K supplements all 
her life; Gitelman's is an autosomal recessive d/o so possible 
could have skipped a generation. Gitelman's usually NOT 
accompanied by hypertension; however, pt's hypertension did not 
start until after he began taking steroids so may be secondary 
hypertension. Primary or secondary hyperaldosteronism also 
possible; can do renin:aldosterone ratio test because even 
though he is on beta blocker this would not affect primary 
hyperaldo (would have high ___ and ___ renin no matter what). 
Surreptitious diuretic use also concerning given that none of 
the symptoms fit a particular clinical picture; however this is 
a diagnosis of exclusion and should not be considered until all 
other potential causes are ruled out. Urine thiazide and loop 
diuretic levels, and renin: ___ ratio were checked and are 
pending on discharge. 

He was treated with potassium supplementation, and his K level 
improved.  He was given a single dose of diuretics, but 
additional doses were held per cardiology recs (discussed with 
his outpatient cardiologist Dr. ___, as patient does not 
have CHF and does not benefit clinically from diuretics. Patient 
will follow up with nephrology, endocrinology and cardiology as 
outpatient. He was discharged with instructions to take KCl 40 
meq daily; K level to be checked again on ___ with 
results sent to Dr. ___.
.
# Weight gain/pedal edema: patient complained of pedal edema and 
weight gain during hospitalization. He did have mild pedal edema 
but in fact was noted to lose one pound over the course of 
hospitalization. Pedal edema suspected to be from steroid 
therapy. 
.
# Premature venttricular beats: pt with PVCs on telemetry and 
EKG on admission, with bigeminy and trigeminy. This has been a 
chronic issue for him. In addition, probably exacerbated by 
hypokalemia. Asymptomatic. Resolved after first day of 
hospitalization.
.
# Acute kidney injury: patient with mild prerenal insufficiency 
on admission. Creatinine resolved to 0.8 on HD #2. 
.
# Diabetes mellitus type 2: patient is on Levemir and ISS with 
carb counting at home. His home insulin regimen was continued 
during hospitalization, with glargine substituted for levemir 
given formulary availability. 
.
